The Korsun Icon of the Mother of God

The Korsun Icon of the Mother of God

Korsunskaya · Cherson icon

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

Luke 1:41–45

King James Version · Scripture previews

The OCA records more than one transfer tradition under the Korsun title, including Vladimir and Euphrosyne of Polotsk.

[1] Published source,paragraph 3; Published source,paragraph 4; Published source,paragraph 5; Published source,paragraph 6

What is depicted

The selected 1867 icon has an elaborate metal covering around Mary and the Child. The file identifies it at the State Hermitage’s Winter Palace church. It is this particular historic example, not a claim that every Korsun image has an identical composition.

History and tradition

One account connects a copy brought from Korsun to Kiev with Vladimir in 988. Another concerns Euphrosyne’s request for an image and its journey from Ephesus through Korsun to Polotsk, followed by association with Toropets. The OCA reports a traditional attribution to Luke; that attribution is not presented as documented authorship for the nineteenth-century work shown here.

[1] Published source,paragraph 3; Published source,paragraph 4; Published source,paragraph 5; Published source,paragraph 6

Published explanation

The published history gives October 9 as the transfer commemoration and preserves the links among Ephesus, Korsun, Polotsk, and Toropets. The profile distinguishes those journeys from the selected museum object’s own provenance, and does not combine differently named copies into one continuously documented panel.

And it came to pass, that, when Elisabeth heard the salutation of Mary, the babe leaped in her womb; and Elisabeth was filled with the Holy Ghost:

And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.

And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?

For, lo, as soon as the voice of thy salutation sounded in mine ears, the babe leaped in my womb for joy.

And blessed is she that believed: for there shall be a performance of those things which were told her from the Lord.

[3] Luke 1:41–45
